141.quote_or_event: “Being infatuated, he is unable to discriminate between the good and the evil. And he is not able to do anything right or proper.”
141.explanation: In explaining why the vows must be guarded, Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi says that unchastity first destroys a person's judgment, and from that come all the other harms.
141.tie_back: Valluvar calls coveting another's wife a folly (பேதைமை) that people who know dharma never fall into, and the Jain commentary likewise calls it a loss of the very power to tell good from evil.
141.source: Tattvārthasūtra 7.9, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi on unchastity (abrahma) (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
141._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. The idea of lust as a failure of discernment is a close match, but the passage is about unchastity in general, not specifically about another man's wife (the following lines do mention 'other women').

142.quote_or_event: “The enjoyment of the man of unstable heart, who under the influence of infatuation approaches his neighbour's wife and sets his affections upon her, while neighbours spread abroad his guilt, and kinsmen dread and mourn, is like (that of the person who takes pleasure in) licking a serpent's head.”
142.explanation: The Jain-authored Nālaṭiyār has a whole chapter on not desiring other men's wives, and this quatrain mocks the man who chases another's wife as a fool tasting pleasure from a serpent's head.
142.tie_back: Valluvar says that of all who stand outside virtue, none is a greater fool than the man who waits at another's door, and the Nālaṭiyār gives that folly its picture: licking a cobra for sweetness.
142.source: Nālaṭiyār 87 (ch. 9, 'The Not Desiring Other Men's Wives'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai
142._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Pope's translation on projectmadurai.org. This is a Tamil Jain text rather than canonical scripture. It matches the folly theme well but has no equivalent of Valluvar's 'standing at the door' wordplay.

143.quote_or_event: “In the assembly he pronounces holy (words), yet secretly he commits sins; but the wise know him to be a deceiver and great rogue.”
143.explanation: In the lecture on 'Knowledge of Women', the Sūtrakṛtāṅga condemns the man who keeps a respectable face in public while secretly sinning with women, and says the wise see through him.
143.tie_back: Valluvar condemns the man who plots against the home of friends who trust him without suspicion, and the Sūtrakṛtāṅga likewise condemns the hidden betrayal of a man who looks trustworthy, though it does not share the Kural's verdict that such a man is 'no different from the dead'.
143.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.4.1.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
143._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org, which labels the page 'Lecture 4: Knowledge of Women, Chapter 2' even though its contents are Jacobi's first chapter. This is a next-best match: it is about hypocrisy, not about betraying a trusting friend, and is addressed to monks.

144.quote_or_event: “Some men of great intelligence who perform their duties as supporters of women, get into their power … (The adulterers’) hands and feet are cut off, their skin and flesh are torn off, they are roasted alive, and acid is poured into their wounds.”
144.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga warns that even men of great intelligence are brought down by illicit passion and then suffer the brutal punishments of the day, and yet, it adds, they 'will not promise not to do the same again'.
144.tie_back: Valluvar asks what a man's greatness is worth if he enters another's home without weighing the wrong even a millet-grain's worth, and the Sūtrakṛtāṅga shows great intelligence counting for nothing once a man is in passion's power.
144.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.4.1.20–21 (cf. 22) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
144._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (the ellipsis joins verses 20 and 21). The match is partial: the text stresses punishment rather than greatness made worthless, and the 'adulterers' label is Jacobi's bracketed gloss.

145.quote_or_event: “If any one see, disgrace lights on the house; if any hand should seize, leg's maimed; in the doing of the shameful deed is dread; it yields as fruit vast hell's affliction: tell me, O profligate, what measure of delight is thine?”
145.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār sets the adulterer's small pleasure against a lasting price: disgrace on the family, bodily punishment, constant dread, and the long suffering of hell as karmic fruit.
145.tie_back: Valluvar says the man who thinks it easy to cross into another's home earns a disgrace that never dies, and the Nālaṭiyār weighs that 'easy' pleasure against disgrace and suffering that follow him into the next life.
145.source: Nālaṭiyār 84 (ch. 9, 'The Not Desiring Other Men's Wives'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai
145._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on projectmadurai.org. This is a Tamil Jain text. It is a strong fit for 'small pleasure, lasting blame', though the Kural speaks of undying disgrace in this world and the Nālaṭiyār mostly of hell.

146.quote_or_event: “Virtue, praise, friendship, greatness, all these four draw not anigh the men who covet their neighbour's wife. Hatred, disgrace and guilt, with fear, these four possessions abide with men who covet their neighbour's wife.”
146.explanation: In its chapter on not desiring other men's wives, the Nālaṭiyār lists the four things the adulterer gains: hatred, disgrace, guilt and fear.
146.tie_back: Valluvar names enmity, sin, fear and disgrace as the four things that never leave the man who wrongs another's home, and the Nālaṭiyār names the same four (பகை, பழி, பாவம், அச்சம்) in almost the same Tamil words.
146.source: Nālaṭiyār 82 (ch. 9, 'The Not Desiring Other Men's Wives'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai
146._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on projectmadurai.org, and the Tamil original repeats the Kural's four words. This is a Tamil Jain text, used because it is almost a one-to-one parallel; the canonical counterpart is Tattvārthasūtra 7.9 (Sarvārthasiddhi: 'hatred and enmity … despicable').

147.quote_or_event: Jain ethics makes 'contentment with one's own wife' (svadārasantoṣa) the fourth of the five minor vows (aṇuvrata) taken by every lay householder. The Tattvārthasūtra lists 'intercourse with an unchaste married woman' among the transgressions that break it.
147.explanation: Jainism asks only monks for total celibacy. For the householder, chastity means being faithful to his own spouse, and this vow is one of the marks of a proper lay follower (śrāvaka).
147.tie_back: Valluvar defines the true householder as the man who does not desire another's wife, and Jainism builds that same restraint into the vows that define its lay householder.
147.source: Tattvārthasūtra 7.28, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
147._accuracy_note: Paraphrased. The wording of 7.28 ('svadārasantoṣa aṇuvrata', 'intercourse with an unchaste married woman') was checked on wisdomlib.org. It is a strong institutional parallel: in both the Kural and Jainism, this restraint is part of what makes a householder.

148.quote_or_event: “While his loving wife dwells in his home, the tender one whom he espoused, — seeking (out an auspicious) day, and sounding the drum, for many folks to know,—and whom he guards as his own, what means a man's glance at another's wife?”
148.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār asks why a man who has publicly married a loving wife should even look at another man's wife, so the restraint begins with the eyes.
148.tie_back: Valluvar calls the man who does not even look (நோக்கா) at another's wife the possessor of 'great manliness', and the Nālaṭiyār likewise puts the moral line at the glance.
148.source: Nālaṭiyār 86 (ch. 9, 'The Not Desiring Other Men's Wives'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai
148._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on projectmadurai.org (I omitted a stray opening quotation mark from the OCR text). This is a Tamil Jain text. Both put the restraint at the gaze, but the Nālaṭiyār argues from contentment with one's own wife rather than celebrating it as heroism.

149.quote_or_event: “Virtue, praise, friendship, greatness, all these four draw not anigh the men who covet their neighbour's wife.”
149.explanation: The first half of this Nālaṭiyār quatrain says that virtue, good name, friendship and greatness all stay away from the man who covets another's wife. Turned around, they belong to the man who does not.
149.tie_back: Valluvar says that those who do not embrace another's wife deserve every good thing in the sea-girt world, and the Nālaṭiyār makes the same point in reverse: virtue, fame, friendship and greatness avoid the man who covets.
149.source: Nālaṭiyār 82, first half (ch. 9, 'The Not Desiring Other Men's Wives'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai
149._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on projectmadurai.org. This is the same quatrain used for Kural 146 (here its first half), because I could not verify a distinct canonical parallel. The fit is reasonable but stated negatively.

150.quote_or_event: In Vimalasūri's Jain Rāmāyaṇa (Paumacariya), Rāvaṇa once paid homage to the omniscient monk Anantavīrya and took a vow never to force himself on any unwilling woman. Even after abducting Sītā, he refuses his queen Mandodarī's urging to use force, because of that vow.
150.explanation: The Jain tradition portrays Rāvaṇa as a great but flawed man who commits grave wrongs, including the abduction itself, yet keeps this one vow about another man's wife. His remaining desire for Sītā still leads to his downfall.
150.tie_back: Valluvar concedes that even a man who does many wrongs should at least not desire another's wife, and the Jain Rāvaṇa is that kind of man: a wrongdoer who still holds a line he has vowed not to cross, though by desiring Sītā at all he falls short of the Kural's ideal.
150.source: Vimalasūri, Paumacariya 14.1–153 (Rāvaṇa's vow) and 46 (Sītā in Laṅkā); summarised in K. R. Chandra, 'A Critical Study of Paumacariyam' (1970), wisdomlib.org
150._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from Chandra's study on wisdomlib.org (the OCR there is partly garbled but clearly records the vow and Rāvaṇa's refusal to use force). The fit is partial: Rāvaṇa still covets and abducts Sītā, so he keeps only the minimum the Kural asks for.
